_comment_model: PRODUCTION TARGET. Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct: 30.5B total / 3.3B active MoE (Qwen3MoeForCausalLM, 48 layers, 128 experts, 8 per token), Apache 2.0, 262k context. Chosen over Qwen3-32B dense and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B because it is code-specialized with a purpose-built function-call format, and our harness is tool-driven and the RL stage is multi-turn tool use. The 3.3B active footprint is what makes it deployable on device: ~10x less compute per token than a 32B dense at comparable memory.
_comment_model_revision: Hub commit b2cff646, resolved 2026-08-03 and verified against the downloaded snapshot: 16 shards, 18,867 tensors, all BF16, 30,532,122,624 parameters, 61,064,245,248 bytes. Without this key model_spec.resolve_model_identity refuses the load outright in production mode (UnpinnedModelError) and, in development, silently trains whatever the shared HF cache happens to hold -- on a cache several people write to, that is not a reproducible run.
_comment_no_midtrain: There is no Base variant of this model, nor of Qwen3-32B or Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Continued pretraining requires one (running it on an instruct model destroys instruction-following -- docs/EVAL_RESULTS.md), and the chat-vector residual requires a base/instruct PAIR. So the cpt recipe cannot reach production at all, and this trains instruct -> SFT -> RL, which is what Dr. Kernel and Kernel-Smith do anyway.
_comment_dataset_path_v5: v5: 207,782 rows / 502,470,043 tokens / 165,047 distinct targets over 11,793 tasks. 61.2% kernel and 38.8% replay by rows, but 14% replay by TOKENS -- which is the unit that matters, and the unit v4 was never measured in. The substantive change from v4 is shape coverage: v4 asked one question (improve this kernel) across all 38,460 of its kernel rows, and this asks six (optimize, repair, PyTorch-to-kernel, spec-to-kernel, dialect port, language), because the benchmark asks five and v4 had zero examples of three of them. Every kernel target passed a numerical gate on real gfx950; 2,806 reward-hacking targets that delegate to torch were removed, along with 81,550 cross-root duplicates and 53,923 redundant repair answers (9.24 per problem down to 1.95). Screened against a frozen index of the evaluation benchmark's own PyTorch sources and against the held-out probe set, neither of which v4 was. output_dir is _v5 so this run cannot overwrite v4 checkpoints. Read from the repository copy on $HOME rather than /shared_nfs: $HOME is shared NFS and visible from every compute node, /shared_nfs is mounted READ-ONLY on the login node so nothing can be staged there from here, and a 1.8GB dataset has none of the size problem that puts output_dir on /shared_nfs. One source of truth, and data/release/reassemble.sh reproduces exactly this file from a fresh checkout.
_comment_dataset_path: v4: 244,732 rows / ~606M estimated tokens (~830M real), built from 82,275 agentic episodes of which 40,590 reached correctness. The AMD-native side is 34,806 step-centric revisions plus 13,572 residual full trajectories -- disjoint by construction, since a full trajectory is emitted only when its episode produced no step row. Measured blend is 65.9% kernel / 21.5% chat / 12.3% coding by tokens, against a 70/17/13 target; chat running over is the safe direction, as the replay literature puts the forgetting-mitigation plateau at 25-30%. Chat replay is Tulu-3 (TuluTalk measures better but its full 808k mixture was never released) and coding replay is OpenCodeReasoning-2, chosen over OpenCodeInstruct because it carries R1 reasoning traces rather than bare instruction->code, and reasoning is the capability replay has to protect here.
_comment_batch: global batch 128 = 2 x 8 x 8 ranks. per_device was 1 on the theory that MoE activation memory tracks the 8 routed experts rather than the 3.3B active figure; the smoke run measured 120GB of 288GB per GPU, so that was over-cautious by more than half. Raising it to 2 halves the micro-batches per optimizer step (16 -> 8), which is where the 119.87 s/step went: the step is dominated by per-micro-batch overhead, not arithmetic. Left at 2 rather than 4 because the smoke measured a 200-row slice at seq 17408, and the full mixture's p90 sequences are longer.
_comment_max_seq_length: 17408 matches the mixture, which is filtered to it. The model supports 262144, but raising this would not add data and would cost activation memory.
_comment_epochs_and_lr: 5e-6 follows the Tulu 3 full-SFT recipe, and this starts from an ALREADY instruction-tuned checkpoint so it warrants being no more aggressive than a recipe meant to instruct-tune a base model; this project has already watched 1e-5 collapse instruction-following once. ONE epoch, not two, and the reason is operational rather than statistical: measured step time is 90-120s, so 2 epochs is ~955 steps = 24-32h, which crosses the 23h walltime and guarantees a requeue. Resuming means reloading from the last checkpoint, and every extra checkpoint is another 976GB rotation peak against ~1011GB free on a SHARED volume. One epoch is ~478 steps = 12-16h, finishes inside a single allocation with no requeue and one mid-run rotation. This is a cold start for RL, which is where the capability actually comes from, so a second epoch is a cheap continuation later if the eval says it is undertrained.
_comment_warmup_ratio: 0.15, not the 0.03 dense default. Qwen3-30B-A3B is a mixture of experts and its ROUTERS are what a short warmup damages: the router is a small linear layer whose argmax decides which experts see gradient at all, so a large early step can collapse it onto a subset of the 128 experts before the loss has told it anything useful, and the experts it stops routing to then receive no gradient to recover with. Published MoE fine-tuning guidance is consistently 0.10-0.15 against 0.03-0.05 for dense. v3 trained at 0.03 and converged, but v3 was 333M tokens against v4's ~1B, so the same ratio is 3x more absolute steps taken before the router is stable.
_comment_max_grad_norm: 0.5, tighter than the 1.0 HF default this config was silently inheriting by not naming it. Same reason as the warmup: routing instability. A gradient spike that would merely be noise in a dense model can permanently re-route tokens in an MoE, and the standard MoE recommendation is half the dense clip. Cheap insurance -- on a healthy run the clip rarely binds, and v3's observed grad_norm sat at 0.2-0.6 with only the warmup spike at 6.05 exceeding it.
_comment_packing: false, and it must stay false while the attention backend is SDPA. Packing concatenates several examples into one sequence and relies on the attention mask to keep them apart; on SDPA that isolation is not reliable and documents cross-contaminate, which degrades quality silently rather than erroring. kore/policy/sft.py already refuses to enable it outside flash_attention_2, and flash_attn is not installed in this venv. The 2-4x throughput it would buy on our 3,377-token mean against a 17,408 limit is real, but not worth a silent correctness risk on the run that feeds RL.
_comment_save: save_total_limit MUST be 1 here. Adam keeps ~16 bytes/param (fp32 weights, grads, m, v), so a 30.5B checkpoint is ~488GB against the 14B's 221GB. At limit=1 a rotation transiently holds two, peaking near 976GB; the volume has ~1090GB free and is SHARED with other users. At limit=2 the peak would be ~1464GB, which does not fit. save_steps is raised to 400 to halve the number of rotation windows, since each one is when the disk is closest to full.
_comment_save_steps: 50. Sized against how runs on this cluster actually END, which is preemption rather than completion: two jobs were killed with SIGTERM (rc=143) at the two-hour mark on a partition running 77 allocated against 2 idle, and v4 is a 2,024-step / ~32h run, so it will be preempted several times before it finishes. At 200 each kill costs up to ~3.2h of training; at 50 it costs up to ~48min. The write itself is ~488GB against 17T free and takes a couple of minutes, so 40 saves over the run is a few percent of wall clock -- cheap against losing hours. save_total_limit=1 keeps the footprint at one checkpoint: the Trainer writes the new one, then deletes the previous, so only the brief rotation window holds two.
_comment_save_only_model: false, deliberately, after establishing what the failure actually was. Run 33992 died at step 400 with 'Disk quota exceeded (os error 122)' having written 4 of 25 shards, and the obvious reading -- a per-user quota we had exhausted -- is wrong. Both volumes are NFSv3 with no quota tooling present, and NFSv3 servers report a FULL VOLUME as EDQUOT. /shared_nfs is shared and its free space swung from ~0 to 5T to 17T within hours of the failure, so the write hit a moment when other users had consumed everything. There is no cap on what we may use. Dropping optimizer state would shrink the write 8x but costs resumability, and buying a smaller failure window by making every failure unrecoverable is the wrong trade when the space is genuinely there: 17T is ~35x one checkpoint and ~17x the 976GB rotation peak. Keep full checkpoints so a killed run resumes instead of restarting.
_comment_fsdp: fsdp_transformer_layer_cls is set explicitly for MoE. With auto_wrap and a null class the policy can wrap at the wrong granularity for Qwen3MoeDecoderLayer, which either shards the 128 experts badly or leaves whole layers unsharded and OOMs.
_comment_output_dir: On /shared_nfs, not /home. A 30B checkpoint is ~488GB and the Trainer writes the new one before deleting the old, so even save_total_limit=1 peaks near 976GB during rotation. /home is a 10TB volume shared with the whole cluster and sat at 310GB free when this was set -- our own footprint is only ~154GB, so the pressure is other users and not something we can reclaim. /shared_nfs has 1,908GB free. Training on /home would have died mid-rotation hours in, having burned the allocation.
_comment_dataset_path: v3: 69,851 rows / ~255M tokens. Adds 4,279 AMD-NATIVE step-centric rows -- single revisions distilled from 11,227 multi-turn trajectories generated on MI355X through KoreEnv against AITER/hipBLASLt production baselines, keeping only correctness-preserving high-gain ones (1,499 fixes, 2,812 speedups). That 22.6% survival rate is the Kernel-Smith filter working as intended: training a local improver means discarding the revisions that were not improvements. Plus 4,493 recovered rows and the 61,079-row v2 base. All three sources passed one decontamination gate with ZERO held-out hits.
